paper_topic: Draft-and-Continue Self-Consistency: a negative result on two-stage branch budgeting for LLM reasoning

nodes.text: Scaling test-time compute has emerged as a powerful paradigm for improving large language model reasoning (Zhu et al., 2025).

Self-consistency (Wang et al., 2022) exemplifies this approach by sampling multiple chain-of-thought reasoning paths (Wei et al., 2022) and aggregating answers via majority vote, achieving substantial accuracy gains over single-sample inference.

However, this effectiveness comes at significant computational cost: generating multiple complete reasoning chains requires proportionally more tokens, making self-consistency expensive for deployment at scale.
nodes.display_label: SC is expensive: many full chains

nodes.text: Recent work has sought to reduce this cost through early stopping and sample pruning strategies.
Confidence-guided early stopping (Aghazadeh et al., 2025) terminates sampling once the posterior probability of the majority answer exceeds a threshold.
Slim-SC (Hong et al., 2025) prunes redundant reasoning chains online using thought embedding similarity.
ESC (Li et al., 2024) applies early stopping based on window vote entropy.
While effective, these approaches fundamentally discard partial reasoning—they stop sampling entirely rather than leveraging the information contained in incomplete chains.
This raises a natural question: can we identify promising reasoning paths early and focus continuation budget on them?

We investigate this question through Draft-and-Continue Self-Consistency (DCS), a two-stage approach that attempts to improve token efficiency by allocating continuation budget to promising branches identified through early voting signals.
In Stage 1, DCS samples B = 7 draft solutions with a token limit Tdraft = 1024, extracts interim answers, and computes a vote histogram.

In Stage 2, it selects k = 3 branches from high-vote answers and continues them for an additional Tcont = 1024 tokens, using a hedge allocation strategy that reserves one slot for the second-place answer to guard against early consensus errors.

Our experiments on MATH-500 with Qwen2.5-Math-7B-Instruct reveal a negative result: DCS matches baseline accuracy (76.8%) but uses 19.6% more tokens than standard self-consistency and 109% more than CGES-LNS, which Pareto-dominates DCS on the accuracy-efficiency frontier.
Analysis reveals that approximately 96% of drafts complete naturally within the token limit, causing the continuation mechanism to rarely activate meaningfully.
We introduce Draft-and-Continue Self-Consistency (DCS), a two-stage approach that attempts to improve efficiency by continuing promising branches rather than stopping early.
We conduct rigorous experiments on MATH-500 comparing DCS against greedy decoding, uniform self-consistency, and confidence-guided early stopping.

We report a negative result with detailed analysis: DCS fails to improve efficiency because high draft completion rates (∼96%) undermine the continuation mechanism, demonstrating that simpler early-stopping methods dominate two-stage approaches when draft budgets are sufficient.

FA0231 is a candid negative-result paper on adaptive compute allocation for self-consistency. Para 1 (N1-N3) sets up Context (test-time compute scaling), the anchor Prior_Work N2 (self-consistency, citations Wang 2022 + Wei 2022), and a Limitation N3 ('However, this effectiveness comes at significant computational cost...') critiquing self-consistency itself. The Limitation N3 has the anchor PW N2 as direct upstream source (PW->L contrast).

Para 2 introduces a Prior_Work cluster: a parent N4 ('Recent work has sought...') and three children N5/N6/N7 (CGES, Slim-SC, ESC) — each is a named cost-reduction technique. They join into Limitation N8 ('these approaches fundamentally discard partial reasoning'). The 'While effective' marker prefaces N8 and applies to all three named techniques, so three contrast edges from N5/N6/N7 -> N8 capture the join. Limitation N9 ('This raises a natural question...') chains from N8 via the consequence marker.

Method block (N10-N12) describes DCS Stage 1 and Stage 2 in concrete terms (B=7, k=3, hedge allocation). Result N13 reports the headline negative finding (DCS uses 19.6% more tokens than SC, 109% more than CGES-LNS); N14 explains the cause (96% draft completion). Three Contributions (C1-C3) close. C3 has an addresses edge back to N8 (the discard-partial-reasoning Limitation that motivated the whole investigation). N4 is a fork (3 PW children); N8 and N14 are joins/forks respectively.
